title: The Puyallup River
text:
Height Above The River
This is a relative elevation model. Instead of height above sea level, each spot shows how far it sits above the nearest river. The downstream slope is removed, so the shape of the floodplain stands out.




River level10 m or more above

title: The Puyallup River
text:
Between Two Rivers
Orting sits between the Puyallup and the braided Carbon, on ground built by mudflows from Mount Rainier. Nearly half of the Orting study area is within 3 m of the river, and the ground southwest of town sits below the leveed Puyallup next to it.

title: The Puyallup River
text:
Rivers That Keep Moving
Comparing LiDAR from 2011 and 2020 shows where the ground changed. Coral is erosion, where banks were cut away. Blue is deposition, where new gravel bars built up.
In nine years the rivers reworked about 1.1 million m³ of sediment. The Carbon below Orting moved the most.

title: The Puyallup River
text:
Scars Of Old Channels
Below Orting the valley widens. Pale curves on the valley floor are old meanders the river left behind, still a little lower than the ground around them.

title: The Puyallup River
text:
Where The White River Joins
At Sumner the White River comes in from the north. It hasn’t always: until a flood in 1906 changed its course, most of the White River flowed north toward Seattle.

title: The Puyallup River
section: A Valley Level With Its River
text:
A Valley Level With Its River

Around Pacific the whole valley floor glows. Almost all of it sits within a meter or two of the White River, the brightest ground anywhere on the map.

title: The Puyallup River
section: A River In A Straight Line
text:
A River In A Straight Line
Downstream, the Puyallup runs straight between levees. The curving scars across the floor show where it used to wander before it was confined.

title: The Puyallup River
text:
Where The Sediment Goes
At the mouth, the river’s sediment builds a delta. Much of the old tideflat is now the Port of Tacoma. Offshore, the seafloor shows the delta front dropping into water more than 150 m deep.

title: The Puyallup River
text:
Built By The River
From Orting to the bay, this valley floor is made of sediment the rivers carried down. Wherever the map glows, the ground is still close to river level.

title: The Puyallup River
text:
How It Was Made


Land
USGS 3DEP 1 m lidar DEMs (Pierce County 2020, King County 2021), resampled to 3 m. Small gaps were filled from the USGS 10 m DEM.


Seafloor
NOAA NCEI CUDEM topobathy, about 3 m, shows the delta front under Commencement Bay.


Rivers
USGS National Hydrography Dataset centerlines for the Puyallup, White and Carbon rivers.


Relative Elevation
The water surface was sampled every 25 m along each river, interpolated across the valley (IDW), smoothed, and subtracted from the DEM, following Daniel Coe’s method.


Change, 2011 To 2020
Pierce County lidar from 2011 and 2020, differenced. A 0.19 m offset measured on stable ground was removed, and change under 0.23 m (the level of detection) was left out.


Map And Story
Python with rasterio, NumPy and matplotlib. Scrollytelling with the Closeread extension for Quarto.

title: Floodplain Height and Channel Erosion of the Puyallup River
text: Orting sits between two rivers carrying heavy sediment loads from Mount Rainier. This project uses LiDAR to map how high the valley floor sits above those rivers, and where the channels have changed between 2011 and 2020.

title: Floodplain Height and Channel Erosion of the Puyallup River
section: How close is the floodplain to the river?
text:
How close is the floodplain to the river?






Relative elevation model: ground height above the nearby river, 2020




 



About 13 km², nearly half the study area, sits within 3 m of the river.
About 5.6 km² sits within 1 m of the river or lower.
The land southwest of Orting sits below the nearby Puyallup. A cross-section shows the ground falling about 4 m away from the leveed channel toward the western bluff.

title: Floodplain Height and Channel Erosion of the Puyallup River
text:
Where did the rivers change?






Elevation change, 2011 to 2020. Red is erosion, blue is deposition.




 



Blue = Deposition: places that got higher, like new gravel bars on the inside of bends or sediment settling in the channel.
Red = Erosion: places that got lower, like banks cut back on the outside of bends.





About 1.1 million m³ of sediment was reworked on dry ground: 625,000 m³ of bank erosion (ground lowered) and 517,000 m³ of deposition (ground built up by new gravel bars).
Overall net change was small (about −107,000 m³), so the rivers mostly moved material around rather than gaining or losing it.
The Carbon below Orting had the most active bank erosion.

title: Floodplain Height and Channel Erosion of the Puyallup River
text:
Data and methods

2020: Pierce County LiDAR (USGS 3DEP), streamed with PDAL, ground modeled with lidR, plus the USGS 1 m DEM for change detection.
2011: Pierce County DTM from the WA DNR Lidar Portal.
REM: river water levels sampled every 25 m, interpolated across the valley (IDW), and subtracted from the DTM.
Change: a 0.19 m vertical offset between surveys was measured on stable ground and removed. Change smaller than 0.23 m (the level of detection) was ignored.

title: Floodplain Height and Channel Erosion of the Puyallup River
text:
Limitations

LiDAR cannot see through water, so change in the wetted channel reflects water level as well as the bed which has been left out of the volume totals.
REM heights are relative to an interpolated water surface, so they’re approximate, especially far from the channel.
